note: Reference library for the frameworks used by The Human Index. 'usage' says whether the app uses the validated items or a custom adaptation. Only Mini-IPIP and SWLS are scored from the published items.

instruments.name: Mini-IPIP
instruments.source: Donnellan, Oswald, Baird & Lucas (2006). Items drawn from the International Personality Item Pool (Goldberg, 1999).
instruments.citation: Donnellan, M. B., Oswald, F. L., Baird, B. M., & Lucas, R. E. (2006). The Mini-IPIP scales: Tiny-yet-effective measures of the Big Five factors of personality. Psychological Assessment, 18(2), 192-203.
instruments.license: IPIP items are in the public domain and free to use, including commercially, without permission (ipip.ori.org).
instruments.methodology: 20 items, four per factor, rated on a 5-point accuracy scale. Items are summed per factor after reverse scoring. Emotional stability is the reverse of the neuroticism items. The app converts each factor to a 0 to 100 position.
instruments.limitations: A short form with fewer items per factor than longer Big Five inventories, so it is less precise and less able to separate facets. Self-report and subject to social desirability and mood. Scores are relative to a scale, not to a population, because this app does not ship population norms for it.
instruments.usageDetail: All 20 items are used with their original wording and 5-point format. Reverse keys are applied through negative dimension weights.

instruments.name: Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS)
instruments.citation: Diener, E., Emmons, R. A., Larsen, R. J., & Griffin, S. (1985). The Satisfaction With Life Scale. Journal of Personality Assessment, 49(1), 71-75.
instruments.license: Free to use, no permission or fee required for research or non-commercial use, as stated by the author (Ed Diener).
instruments.methodology: 5 statements rated 1 to 7 (strongly disagree to strongly agree). Items are summed to a total from 5 to 35. The original paper reported high internal consistency (alpha about .87) and two-month test-retest stability (about .82) in student samples.
instruments.limitations: Measures a global cognitive judgement of life, not day-to-day mood. Sensitive to current circumstances and to cultural norms about expressing satisfaction. It does not diagnose anything. The app pairs it with a separate 'past two weeks' mood item to help separate a passing state from a longer-term view.
instruments.usageDetail: All five items are used verbatim with the 7-point format and are interpreted on the raw 5 to 35 sum.

instruments.name: Holland occupational themes (RIASEC)
instruments.citation: Holland, J. L. (1997). Making vocational choices: A theory of vocational personalities and work environments (3rd ed.). Psychological Assessment Resources.
instruments.license: The theory is freely usable. Commercial inventories built on it (for example the Strong Interest Inventory and Self-Directed Search) are copyrighted, and their items are not used here.
instruments.methodology: Six interest types describe preferences for kinds of activities and settings. People are often summarised by their top three letters. Career suggestions come from matching a person's profile to the types associated with an occupation.
instruments.limitations: Interests are not the same as ability, opportunity or pay. The model is a simplification, and an occupation can fit several profiles. Interest profiles also shift as people gain experience.
instruments.usageDetail: The app uses its own activity statements, rankings and ratings for each type. It does not use the items of any published interest inventory, so scores are exploratory and not comparable with other RIASEC tools.

instruments.name: PERMA model of wellbeing
instruments.source: Seligman (2011); Butler & Kern (2016) for the PERMA-Profiler
instruments.citation: Seligman, M. E. P. (2011). Flourish. Free Press. Butler, J., & Kern, M. L. (2016). The PERMA-Profiler: A brief multidimensional measure of flourishing. International Journal of Wellbeing, 6(3), 1-48.
instruments.license: The model is a published framework. The PERMA-Profiler is made available by its authors for research use, and its items are not reproduced here.
instruments.methodology: Wellbeing is described through five building blocks: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishment.
instruments.limitations: PERMA is a conceptual model, and the five elements overlap. Its status as a complete account of wellbeing is debated. Single custom items give a rough signal, not a validated score.
instruments.usageDetail: One to three custom items per element, written for this app. Scores are exploratory and not comparable with the PERMA-Profiler.

instruments.name: Self-Determination Theory (SDT)
instruments.citation: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist, 55(1), 68-78.
instruments.license: The theory is freely usable. Related scales are made available by the SDT authors for research use and are not reproduced here.
instruments.methodology: SDT proposes three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence and relatedness) and distinguishes motivation that comes from interest and meaning from motivation that comes from rewards or pressure.
instruments.limitations: Motivation is usually mixed, and a person can be driven by both kinds at once. Choice questions such as 'successful in a disliked career or moderate in a loved one' force a trade-off that real life rarely does.
instruments.usageDetail: Custom items and scenarios inspired by the theory. The app does not use the Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction scales.

instruments.name: Schwartz theory of basic values
instruments.source: Schwartz (1992); Schwartz et al. (2001) for the Portrait Values Questionnaire
instruments.citation: Schwartz, S. H. (1992). Universals in the content and structure of values. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 25, 1-65. Schwartz, S. H., et al. (2001). Extending the cross-cultural validity of the theory of basic human values with a different method of measurement. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 32(5), 519-542.
instruments.license: The theory is freely usable. The Schwartz Value Survey and Portrait Values Questionnaire are made available by the author for research use, and their items are not reproduced here.
instruments.methodology: Values are motivational goals that can support or conflict with one another, for example freedom and security. Rankings and forced trade-offs reveal priorities more reliably than ratings, because most values are rated as important.
instruments.limitations: The app's 15-value list is a short, informal selection, not the full Schwartz model. Stated values can differ from lived values. Rankings are relative, so a low rank does not mean a value is unimportant.
instruments.usageDetail: A custom list of 15 values, ranked in two sets and tested in dilemmas. Informed by Schwartz but not scored as the Schwartz Value Survey.

instruments.name: Achievement goal orientation
instruments.citation: Dweck, C. S., & Leggett, E. L. (1988). A social-cognitive approach to motivation and personality. Psychological Review, 95(2), 256-273. Elliot, A. J., & McGregor, H. A. (2001). A 2 x 2 achievement goal framework. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(3), 501-519.
instruments.license: Published theory. The scales from these papers are not used.
instruments.methodology: People can pursue tasks to learn and improve (mastery) or to show competence relative to others (performance). Mastery orientation tends to go with persistence after setbacks.
instruments.limitations: Orientation can change with context. Few people are purely one or the other. Single items give only a rough indication.
instruments.usageDetail: Two custom items plus indirect evidence from related choices. Exploratory only.

instruments.name: Self-efficacy
instruments.source: Bandura (1977); Schwarzer & Jerusalem (1995) for the General Self-Efficacy Scale
instruments.citation: Bandura, A. (1977). Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change. Psychological Review, 84(2), 191-215. Schwarzer, R., & Jerusalem, M. (1995). Generalized Self-Efficacy scale. In J. Weinman, S. Wright, & M. Johnston (Eds.), Measures in health psychology (pp. 35-37). NFER-NELSON.
instruments.license: The theory is freely usable. The General Self-Efficacy Scale is free for non-commercial use per its authors, and its items are not reproduced here.
instruments.methodology: Self-efficacy is the belief that one can carry out the actions needed to reach a goal. It is usually domain-specific, which is why the app asks about general, social and professional confidence separately.
instruments.limitations: Beliefs can be inaccurate in either direction. High self-efficacy does not guarantee skill, and low self-efficacy can improve with experience.
instruments.usageDetail: Custom items worded in the spirit of the theory. Scores are exploratory.

instruments.name: Attachment-related tendencies
instruments.source: Brennan, Clark & Shaver (1998), Experiences in Close Relationships
instruments.citation: Brennan, K. A., Clark, C. L., & Shaver, P. R. (1998). Self-report measurement of adult attachment: An integrative overview. In J. A. Simpson & W. S. Rholes (Eds.), Attachment theory and close relationships (pp. 46-76). Guilford Press.
instruments.license: Published research. The ECR items are not reproduced here.
instruments.methodology: Adult attachment is often described along two dimensions: worry about being abandoned and discomfort with closeness.
instruments.limitations: Tendencies vary by relationship and over time. The app uses a handful of custom items and does not assign an attachment 'style'.
instruments.usageDetail: Custom items inspired by the two-dimension view. Never reported as a type or label.

instruments.name: Enjoyment motives (hobby discovery)
instruments.citation: None. Informed loosely by intrinsic motivation research (Ryan & Deci, 2000) and flow research (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990).
instruments.methodology: The person picks activities and then says why they enjoy them. The reasons, not the activities, drive hobby suggestions.
instruments.limitations: Not validated. It reflects what a person says draws them to activities they already know, so it can miss what they have never tried.
